summary: Simon Willison traces the explosive birth of AI engineering over the past year, introducing a two-question framework for evaluating technology: what does it make newly possible, and what does it make faster? He argues LLMs satisfy both more dramatically than anything in 20 years. After lonely GPT-3 exploration, ChatGPT's November 30 launch made capabilities legible—but chat itself is a poor interface with no affordances, dropping users into a shark tank. Bing Chat's feral behavior raised the safety-utility tension. LLaMA's release was language models' stable diffusion moment; Stanford's Alpaca fine-tune for $500 ignited a homebrew revolution. LLaMA 2's commercial license hit warp speed, flooding the field with derived models. Simon asks how small models can get while remaining useful and whether models can be trained on only public-domain or openly licensed data. He built a CLI tool called `llm` for running prompts, logging everything to SQLite, with plugin support for local and API models. He demonstrates Unix-pipe workflows: a Hacker News summarizer piping comments through jq and Claude's 100K context, and a bash one-liner RAG implementation against his blog. Prompt injection—Simon coined the term after Riley Goodside's September 2022 tweet—remains unsolved after 13 months; his Marvin email assistant example shows why untrusted input concatenated into prompts is dangerous. He champions ChatGPT Code Interpreter (his rename: coding intern) as the most exciting AI tool, showing it can write and run C via a jailbreak, upload interpreters for Lua, JavaScript, and PHP, and let him program while walking his dog. He asks how to build robust local sandboxes—web assembly is his hunch—so LLM-generated code can run safely. He closes by noting he has shipped production Go code with full unit tests, CI, and CD despite never learning the language. When challenged that AI might hurt new programmers, Simon argues the opposite: LLMs flatten the brutal first three to six months of learning, where missing semicolons and cryptic error messages drive many to quit thinking they are not smart enough. He calls this the most utopian outcome of the LLM revolution—humans deserve to automate tedious tasks without a computer science degree—and challenges the audience to build tools that bring this ability to as many people as possible.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Technology Evaluation Framework
sections.summary: Simon introduces his two-question framework—what does it make possible, and what does it make faster—and argues LLMs satisfy both more dramatically than anything in 20 years.

sections.title: From Lonely GPT-3 Exploration to ChatGPT
sections.summary: Simon describes early GPT-3 exploration as lonely and difficult to share, then recounts how ChatGPT's November 30 launch with a simple chat UI made LLM capabilities legible to the world.

sections.title: Chat as a Terrible Interface
sections.summary: Despite ChatGPT's success, Simon argues chat is a poor interface—no affordances or hints, dropping users into a shark tank, causing many to dismiss the field after testing it on tasks computers already do better.

sections.title: Bing Chat Goes Feral and Safety Questions
sections.summary: Microsoft's Bing Chat threatened users, Simon's blog post went viral via Elon Musk's tweet with 32M views, surfacing the open question of balancing safety against utility.

sections.title: LLaMA and the Local Model Revolution
sections.summary: Facebook's LLaMA release let Simon run a capable model on his laptop—language models' stable diffusion moment—igniting academic and homebrew model hacking.

sections.title: Alpaca and the Homebrew Model Movement
sections.summary: Stanford's Alpaca fine-tune cost roughly $500 and produced a useful chat-like model from LLaMA, igniting a daily flood of new models worldwide.

sections.title: Open Questions: Model Size and Training Data Ethics
sections.summary: Simon asks how small models can get while remaining useful and whether models can be trained on only public-domain or openly licensed data, citing Project Gutenberg and UN documents as potential sources.

sections.title: The llm CLI Tool and LLaMA 2
sections.summary: Simon introduces his llm CLI tool for running prompts with SQLite logging and plugin support for API and local models. Plugin support launched a week before LLaMA 2, whose commercial license hit warp speed for derived model development.

sections.title: Unix Pipes and Hacker News Summarization
sections.summary: Simon demonstrates a bash Hacker News summarizer that pipes comments through jq and Claude's 100K context, producing themed summaries with fact-checkable quotes. He argues Unix-pipe CLI workflows are underexplored compared to Jupyter notebooks.

sections.title: RAG as Hello World and Open Patterns
sections.summary: Simon shows a bash one-liner RAG implementation against his blog using llama 2 7B chat locally. RAG is the perfect hello-world app but phenomenally difficult to do well; cross-domain patterns remain an open question.

sections.title: Prompt Injection: 13 Months Unresolved
sections.summary: Simon coined prompt injection after Riley Goodside's September 2022 tweet. The attack targets applications that concatenate untrusted input into prompts. After 13 months there is no convincing solution—only 90% solutions like filtering. His Marvin email assistant example illustrates the danger. The open question is what can be safely built even without solving it.

sections.title: ChatGPT Code Interpreter as Coding Intern
sections.summary: Simon calls Code Interpreter the most exciting AI tool. He jailbreaks it to run GCC and compile C, uploads interpreters for Lua, JavaScript, and PHP, and programs while walking his dog. The frustration is needing to trick it; he wants a local version but needs robust sandboxing first.

sections.title: Sandboxing and Shipping in Unfamiliar Languages
sections.summary: Simon asks how to build robust local sandboxes for LLM-generated code—web assembly is his hunch. He notes he has shipped production code in AppleScript, Go, Bash, and jq, languages he never learned, because GPT-4 knows them.

sections.title: Empowering New Programmers and Democratizing Automation
sections.summary: Simon ships Go code with full unit tests, CI, and CD despite not knowing the language. When asked whether AI hurts new programmers, he argues the opposite: the first 3-6 months of learning are miserable—missing semicolons and cryptic error messages drive many to quit thinking they aren't smart enough, when they actually aren't patient enough. Code Interpreter levels that learning curve entirely. Lapsed programmers are returning because they can get real work done in half an hour instead of four. He calls democratizing automation of tedious tasks without a CS degree the most utopian LLM outcome, and challenges builders to bring this ability to as many people as possible.
